method: Questions were researched with an evidence-only retrieval tool over one corpus of open-access and public-domain texts (see corpus.json). Each excerpt was checked word for word against the corpus passage it cites when this file was written; corpus_chunk numbers that passage in the corpus snapshot of 2026-10-01.
questions: What makes a collection of propositions an argument?
How do arguments differ from explanations, conditionals and implications?

evidence.excerpt: A collection of propositions, P1, …, Pn, C, is an argument if and only if there is a reasoner R who puts forward the Pi as reasons in support of C.
The structure of an argument is not a function of the syntactic and semantic features of the propositions that compose it. Rather, it is imposed on these propositions by the intentions of a reasoner

(i) The premises represent R’s reasons for believing that the conclusion is true and R thinks that her belief in the truth of the premises is justified. (ii) R believes that the premises make C more probable than not.
R believes that the premises are independent of C
B’s assertion of a conditional does not require that B believe either the antecedent or consequent.
Even though few syphilis patients get paresis, we suspect that the reason for your uncle’s paresis is the syphilis he suffered from 10 years ago.
B: Bill will be at the party, because Bill will be at the party.
Whereas the act of explaining is designed to increase the audience’s comprehension, the act of arguing is aimed at enhancing the acceptability of a standpoint.

in presenting an argument the reasoner believes that her standpoint is not yet acceptable to her audience, but in presenting an explanation the reasoner knows or believes that the explanandum is already accepted by her audience
It is generally accepted that the same line of reasoning can function as an explanation in one dialogical context and as an argument in another
these expressions do not always function in these ways, and so their mere use does not necessitate the presence of an argument
an argument is merely a list of statements, one of which is designated as the conclusion and the rest of which are designated as premises regardless of whether the premises are offered as reasons
The proposition frogs are mammals implies that frogs are not reptiles, but it is problematic to offer the former as a reason for believing the latter.
an inference is a form of reasoning, and as such it is distinct from an argument in the sense of a collection of propositions
arguments can be constructed for purposes of inquiry and as such can be used to investigate a hypothesis by seeing what reasons might be given to support a given proposition
a reasoner can offer premises for a conclusion C in order to get her audience to withhold assent from C, suspect that C is true
follow those who think that at least some explanations qualify as arguments (see Thomas 1986 who argues that all explanations are arguments)
some argue that a fully comprehensive account of real-life argument must include a “multimodal” account of meaning
gestures, facial expressions, sounds of different sorts
